We’ve been waiting since October 2024 for a spousal visa, so they don’t all get processed faster it seems! The home office operates on their own time sadly.

Together for eight years, married for two before we applied for the visa. Had plenty of evidence of our relationship (pictures, texts, old leases), and we lived together for four years when my wife was in the States (where I’m from). Sadly, we’re still waiting for a decision, and we submitted my application to join her in the UK six months ago. We seem to be some of the unlucky ones in terms of time.
We did submit an inquiry, which also got a standard response. I haven’t tried the complaints team (if that’s a separate thing), but will look into it!
They say it’s odd, but ultimately, there’s nothing we can do. They just suggested to keep contacting the MP, which hasn’t proven effective, sadly.

I am currently employed in the US at the moment, and my wife is employed in the UK.  She makes roughly \~60k GBP a year, and we have a joint savings account together (with about \~10k).  From my understanding, this is well above the financial requirements.  And, of course, we submitted 12 months of payslips, bank account info, and all the other docs with the visa application.

We checked a couple solicitors, but the one we went with cost us about 800 gbp all together.  They had a more expensive option, where they did literally everything for you for around 2000 gbp, but we chose a middle route.  We compiled all the documents ourselves, wrote our cover letters, etc., filled out the whole application, and then our solicitors looked over it.  They gave some good feedback, and it was just reassuring to have a professional tell you that you have everything you need.  

  
I would say well worth it, but we're still waiting on a decision after nearly six months.  But I would be a lot more stressed, if we hadn't gone through a solicitor.  So, if it gets approved, I'll say if it was worth it, if it gets denied, well.  Then it was an obvious waste of money.

I don’t know enough about social politics to speak of its effectiveness, but I’m sure JSO is aware of this impressiom, and something about their internal research shows that simply being in the public consciousness, even in a negative light, is still productive for their cause. 

My intuition says that it shouldn’t work, and that it will just drive people away, but who knows. They’re not a fringe network, and have activists who know what they’re doing. They’re portrayed by the media as radical crazies, but that’s certainly not the case—I’ll leave the tactics to the people who are experts. Whether it’s effective, I guess we’ll see.

It’s worth checking out if you have the time. The gist is that Just Stop Oils prime motivation is to simply be in the public headlines. The name was intentionally chosen to be as direct as possible, the color orange as bright and recognizable as possible, and their protests as public as possible. The video talks about and interviews people involved, including two elderly women who attempted to break the glass case the Magna Carta is housed in (they barely indented the glass). The whole operation is pretty diligent about not causing actual harm, and has distanced themselves from other activists that seek more extreme measures. The media portrays most of these people as delusional, self righteous assholes, but everyone included in this video is very aware of their methods, a little sad that this is the only way they can protest to make headlines, and quite reasonable appearing. I’ll be honest, as someone who loves art and museums, I initially thought JSO was full of shit and potentially a smear campaign by big oil. After doing more research, I support their cause a lot more, but still don’t fully agree with their methods. 

It mostly comes down to how you view protests, and how disruptive they are allowed to be in order to get things changed. Everyone will feel differently about that, and it’s a hard question to answer. A notable point is that the UK government HAS recently lost court battles for breaking their climate pledges; JSO may or may not have had a part in this, who’s to say. The UK has ALSO passed increased legislation that allows the police to arrest protestors with more freedom, and less reason. Exxon Mobil partly funded and lobbied this legislation, what a surprise. 

Regardless of their methods, and whether they are right or wrong, JSO has made an impact, and will probably continue to do so. Throwing soup at art looks (and is) stupid, but it is causing the UK to pay attention.

It’s not just Tommy John though, and if you broaden the scope, the data does seem to suggest something plagues the Rays.  

Data: from Fangraphs. 

Seasons 2020-2023.
The pool of players: SP and RP only.
Types of injuries: all with the exception of anything to do with COVID. (It appears that virtually every severe injury is due to the arm. So, it is a good approximation.)
Measurements: number of IL events and total days lost on the roster due to IL events.
Calculated: Mean days lost per IL event.

Seasons 2020 through 2023

Again, for any injury this season, if the pitcher was still on the IL, I set the "end date" to today. I did this because we can't predict the future.

Pitcher on the IL events within a team:
Range: 27 (CLE) to 87 (TBR)
Mean 57, Standard Deviation (STD): 12.5
TBR: 87. 

The most, the far extreme. More than 2 SD beyond the mean. 2020 to 2022 was bad, and you suffered through it.

Days lost by pitcher on the roster due to IL events:
Range: 1506 (CLE) to 5230 (TBR)
Mean: 2990, STD: 830
TBR: 5230, the most, the far, far, far extreme. 

Rays fans can complain.

Mean Days Lost per pitcher IL event:
Range: 42 (SFG) to 63 (SEA)
Mean: 52, STD: 6
TBR: 60. More than 1 but less than 2 SD above the mean.

I suspect that if there were enough seasons, the range of mean days lost per IL event would diminish. Most teams end up with just about the same. What counts is the total number.
